searchText: 'Dada' means" big brother" And 'होउ de merge ' means "Let it merge" "एथेरियम मित्रमंडली" means "Ethereum community" And "आला रे आला panda आला" means "Comming comming panda is comming" lol. it's <@425274498732916736> who's depicted as <@552133098075193354> 😂 Here is Indian <@273808422753796097> 😅 Why isn’t having clients hit a URL under the Ethereum foundation’s domain for a dynamic TTD a default option? It pretty much contains the same trust assumptions as accepting a baked into the code TTD does and you still have the option to force an override What if the domain gets hacked? Things like that happen. Not only because of EF's fault, but someone might social engineer the domain registrar. Baked into the code means that client devs define it, and each client dev *can* define it independently, and at time of update the user can verify/validate and it then cannot change out from under the user. There is a very big difference in trust between a one-time trust operation that can be validated through a trust network and an ongoing trust relationship that can be compromised at any time (which means you cannot validate it through your trust network without a similar continuous validation process). +1 to Micah, also the massive risk of bugs in using a completely untested approach to set parameters. will mev boost be available for all clients @ merge? that is the stated goal great, otherwise client diversity thingy will come back again <:blob_sweat:792417931425218580> indeed very high incentive to ship mev-boost for CL clients Does anyone have the Sepolia Merge block (first validator-produced block with an `ExecutionPayload`) handy? you want the ssz? https://sepolia.beaconcha.in/block/115193 no, just the number so we can use it for the official merge block 🙂 https://twitter.com/Gajpower/status/1545437029927817217 you can always hard code an EF public key into the code, and encrypt the TTD value. And have fallbacks, so 1) override flag 2) url 3) default hard coded TTD value sure, but realistically speaking, after the code has been compiled and for 99% of the users, nobody would be able to verify anything. so either way you're taking it on faith to a degree, and like i mentioned above if an emergency change of TTD is needed, i would think its better to have a way of controlling with a secondary fallback all clients rather than hoping your mass communication is effective enough to make a large enough group of people use the override flag with the correct number something that has proven in Sepolia to be especially hard... (boggles the mind... but hey, something something about the irrationality of markets) i think what i described above was addressing the notion that realistically, we do not have an emergency last minute, time is of the essence way, to have a large group of validators change their TTD if we needed it. for a one time event, I didn't think the trust tradeoff was so great. I think several of the clients have deterministic build systems, so it can be verified. Also, trust networks are key here. You don't need to verify the code, you just need someone in your extended trust network who verifies the code and can get a warning out to you prior to the merge. Ideally we can get to a point where the released TTD is what can be used, and we don't need to get clients to change it late in the game... _if_ we wanted dynamic config control for TTD or other values, wouldn't it make more sense for that to be output via logs/events from a smart contract and watched on-chain like the deposit info? (vs. an external endpoint) ^ keyword: if 🙂 fair point, and definitely a big IF is it really an if? can we afford to not have a last minute emergency way to push a ttd into clients? <dannyryan> There is an emergency flag in place From my perspective its much simpler to do what we're doing now where we communicate a change to TTD, so i'd probably stick with that unless there's a compelling reason to do something else again, heavily relying on trust if we assume that 33% of the validators lay between Lido and maybe Coinbase and we have contacts in both, then sure. But if 33% of the validators are fragmented what stops a Sepolia case from happening again? didn't it prove our communication methods insufficient? if you believe some of the metrics floating about, then lido is around 31%, coinbase around 14%, but i mean this is no different to a major client having a build that's incorrect i just dont want to be making solutions that have to go looking for a problem either didn't the problem reveal itself though? reading TTD from an external source (on or off chain) could be proof-of-concepted outside of clients (e.g. a wrapper that detects a new TTD config and injects it into the client config and restarts it), so technically no buyin is needed by the devs to implement at least a proof on concept. randomness happened i think a better description would be 'life happened' as in, that's how much you can trust humans in the loop. that's the thing with chaos, if it happened this time, will it happen again, or is it just chaos if said POC proves useful then perhaps the client devs can be convinced, but IMO thats a better way to sell the idea than to try to get all the client devs to agree on a last-minute external TDD source spec. fair point i think with people controlling large numbers of validators, we really want to try to avoid having late hcanges to ttd if at all possible ideally we can bake in a number and just have to give ourselves more wiggle / wait time which i know is annoying to have to wait longer than a few hours, but its certainly less chaotic than late ttd changes i fully agree <@680234424037670912> i just hope it doesn't come back to hunt us with miners deciding to call it quits earlier than we expect them to oh - yes that could be interesting a robust system that can handle that would be complicated and a vector of issues... difficult choice this far down the line I guess i kind of expect miners to be mining until the last block, because it's all money... pulling the pin early is literally saying no to cash... whoever stays around is likely to win big in that scenario... I could be wrong 🙂 except that right now, i believe (i could be wrong myself here) most miners are already losing money with crypto prices where they're at... and there's really no shortage of crypto coins to mine these days i also don't think we know what a critical amount of miners need to decide to drop off before this becomes a problem for our baked in TTD if its sufficiently long then another release would be a viable option realistically if our only problem during merge turns out to be TTD needing to change, things have probably not ended in a dumpster fire but admittedly 400k validators needing to restart is sub-optimal that's my thinking... Sepolia is highly centralized compared to Mainnet and we couldn't even communicate a single flag change there. nothing earth shattering.... and aimed at mostly professional crowd. Good luck with the home crowed spread across 400k validators in anything resembling a timely manner. most test nets have needed to change TTD and seem to go ok... Sepolia was highly centralised but also brand new and highly disorganised. A lot of clients didn’t have a stable release out with the final config at all for example. We have had cases where very last minute changes needed to happen with MainNet upgrades - most notably cancelling Constantinople and it worked well. People pay a lot more attention to MainNet than they do testnets. Seems reasonable to undershoot the TTD if you think hashrate will drop off? I guess there's a lot of factors that'll go into the decision making...

excerpts.author: schone_wizard
excerpts.content: Why isn’t having clients hit a URL under the Ethereum foundation’s domain for a dynamic TTD a default option? It pretty much contains the same trust assumptions as accepting a baked into the code TTD does and you still have the option to force an override

excerpts.author: Deleted User
excerpts.content: What if the domain gets hacked? Things like that happen. Not only because of EF's fault, but someone might social engineer the domain registrar.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Baked into the code means that client devs define it, and each client dev *can* define it independently, and at time of update the user can verify/validate and it then cannot change out from under the user.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: There is a very big difference in trust between a one-time trust operation that can be validated through a trust network and an ongoing trust relationship that can be compromised at any time (which means you cannot validate it through your trust network without a similar continuous validation process).
